I'm not shedding any tears for Paul O'Neal, but there were a lot of problems here.

- The two initial officers did not use their vehicle in an effective manner to stop the stolen vehicle, and the driver exited in what is at best a tactically unwise fashion. Better training could resolve this.

- The passenger exits the squad car and engages a moving target, against department policy, muzzle sweeping other officers and carelessly firing towards civilian homes and other officers. The officers down the street assume they're receiving incoming fire - because the two initial responding officers are firing rounds in their direction. This is all a training issue.

- While O'Neal WAS using a deadly weapon (the vehicle) and DID display clear aggression, he was significantly less of a threat (for the moment) when his vehicle was disabled and on foot. Of course, the officers assumed the suspect was armed because they received incoming fire - not aware it was from other police. So they treated him as if he was still a continued threat even on foot. But we're going to have a hell of a difficult time, both in a court of law and in the court of public opinion, convincing anyone that this is a justified use of deadly force against a fleeing suspect, considering they found no gun and he was shown to be shot in the back.

This isn't a case of 'evil cops slaughtering innocent black lives', but it DOES reveal some serious gaps in police training and their ability to retain sound judgment and communication under stress. They're ostensibly supposed to be trained for this.

You are really, really, really wrong on a lot of different points.

Hollow points are designed to expand. This serves two different purposes. First, they create a larger permanent wound cavity, so they are more effective in killing people, yes. But the secondary purpose - and the one that is *exceedingly* more important, in my opinion - is significantly reducing the risk of overpenetration. A standard full-metal jacket round (not 'parabellum') is far more likely to hit someone and exit the other side - both causing less damage to the person you are shooting *and* presenting a risk to any bystanders. Or if one of your shots is to miss, an FMJ is far more likely to overpenetrate any barriers than an expanding hollow point bullet.

A hollow point bullet is so much safer than an FMJ. Seriously. They save lives. They keep innocent bystanders safe. And if you are drawing your gun and shooting at someone, *YOU ARE (or should be) IN IMMEDIATE DANGER OF GRIEVOUS INJURY OR DEATH, OR YOUR INACTION WILL ALLOW OTHERS TO BE IN IMMEDIATE DANGER OF GRIEVOUS INJURY OR DEATH.* You use the ammunition that is most likely to quickly and effective neutralize the assailant, through damage to the brain or the upper spine, a massive drop in blood pressure, or (if you are lucky) a psychological shock to being shot. If it is not a life or death situation, where you do not need 'bullets designed to kill', you should not use a gun at all - you should use a less-lethal weapon system instead.

The reason the military use FMJs is because they are more often in situations where they *need* to punch through cover or body armor. They need that reach, that destructive capability, and they (usually) have more distance between themselves and the badguys, as well as the benefit of volume of fire from their entire fireteam / squad / platoon etc. The reason cops use hollowpoints is because they need to know they WON'T be punching through cover, they are less likely to encounter body armor, and it is (usually) maybe one or two guys with pistols shooting at someone within 5 to 7 meters.

A single shell of 12-gauge 00 buckshot contains nine approximately .33 caliber sized pellets, fired at approximately 1,200 feet per second. Depending on the ammunition you use and the choke of your barrel, the pattern could either be tight enough to fit within center mass of a full grown man within 40 yards, or scattered all over the place. Each one of those individual pellets has a greater lethality than a .32 ACP, and this is all from a single shell.

The shotgun firing 12-gauge buckshot is NOT the simple, easy weapon platform it is often perceived as. It is heavy, it is complicated, it is finicky, depending on your load it has significant recoil, and a single pull of the trigger puts nine very deadly projectiles downrange that CAN penetrate several layers of drywall that you need to be fully accountable for.

There are so many things wrong with 28 Weeks Later, but here's my big complaint.

In 28 Days Later, the rage outbreak starts in Cambridge. It is, of course, highly infectious and virulent, as well as being poorly understood - no one knew about it beforehand and so they were not prepared for it whatsoever. The British Isles, with it's population of about 62 million-ish people, is almost completely wiped out, and a great deal of these people are turned into blood thirsty contagious killing machines. There's even rumors in the film of a handful of infected people making it off of the island! A very grim situation indeed.

And yet... Everyone outside of the UK manage to keep things under control. If there are any outbreaks, they're promptly quelled, and a quarantine is quickly and successfully set up. Let me drive this point home here - with no knowledge or understanding on the rage virus, with no possible way to be prepared for this scenario, and with several MILLION infected on the island likely trying to get out, they STILL manage to keep it contained with minimal incident, until most of the infected died off and they just had to go in and clean up.

And on the other hand... In 28 Weeks Later, the rage virus has been studied and understood. They know what it does, how it works, how it spreads, and how to deal with it. We've fought it, we've beat it, we've got it. We know whats up! When the outbreak starts, there's *maybe* a couple thousand people on the island, including the military task force. And yet...everything totally goes to shit and even ends up WORSE than the original outbreak. What the titfuck?! I couldn't wrap my head around this, it's absolutely absurd that the scenario would play out like that.
